record.file_problem: The full post text is present. Referenced figures are not included in the supplied text.
record.tranche_reason: Tests toy-model feature representation with a different model and objective from the original: it removes the ReLU, changes the loss to target-only reconstruction, and uses 100 inputs. The results bear on superposition and feature capacity, but do not reproduce the original setup.
record.gate_note: The post reports that a target-only loss allows a linear toy model to represent more feature classes than its two-dimensional space has dimensions, with results depending on p. The p values define training conditions and are not merely selection settings. The cited papers and the comments' claims are not results from this study; referenced figures are unavailable here, so only results stated in the post are recorded.
record.test_reason: The post builds a modified toy model (no ReLU, target-only loss, 100 features in 2-D) to argue that two TMS-derived assumptions do not hold universally. These are that feature count is bounded by nearly-orthogonal packing, and that superposition needs element-wise nonlinearities. It reports feature-representation counts for this model, which bear on V1's account of how and when features are superposed in small networks.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also explicitly claim to show that two assumptions are not universally true. The first is that feature count is bounded by the number of nearly-orthogonal vectors. The second is that element-wise nonlinearities are what make superposition possible. They argue the ReLU in TMS mainly filters interference rather than computing. They concede the target-only loss does 'heavy lifting' and acts as a covert selection step.
record.recipe_differences: This is an alternative toy-model experiment, not a reproduction: it removes the ReLU, uses a target-only squared reconstruction loss, and expands from five to 100 input features.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported feature-class accuracy differs with p: the authors say increasing sparsity makes accurate representation easier; p=0 permits more than 50 accurate features, while p=0.95 yields 31.
record.problems: The authors say the experiments were done quickly, took roughly 30 hours, and are not rigorous or confidently established. The target-only loss is explicitly acknowledged as unconventional and as doing substantial work; the post does not report uncertainty estimates or a control model. The supplied text omits the referenced figures.
record.rows_left_out: No separate rows for cited work or comments: these are not results from the authors' experiment. No figure-only values were available in the supplied text.

untested.parts: The original setting (ReLU, full MSE loss) is not systematically tested. There are no measurements of pairwise angles, regular polytope geometry, or a mapped sparsity phase transition. Only two p values are reported, from single runs.
Not tested: there is no comparison of one-dimensional with multi-dimensional features.

missing.what: Qualitative reproduction of the original TMS model: it does not always represent all five features, though successful runs are clean.

record.verdict_notes: Informal LessWrong post with about 30 hours of work. The authors disclaim confidence, report single runs, and give no uncertainty estimates. A commenter (StefanHex) argues the target-only loss ignores interference on inactive features, making the task unrealistically easy and arguably not superposition in the TMS sense; the author concedes the setting is entirely different. Tranche set to T5 rather than T2 because the stated aim is to argue that a TMS claim needs restating. The p values are training conditions, not selection values.

versions.untested_parts: The study reports feature-class accuracy under a different objective, but does not quantify pairwise angles or establish that the directions are nearly orthogonal or have regular geometry. Its p=0 setting has no non-target coactivation; p=0.95 is not a sparse coactivation setting.

The toy model uses scalar input features represented by directions, but the study does not compare one-dimensional features with multidimensional features or establish which feature dimensionality is general.

source_check.reason: R1 and R2 support qualifying generalizations of V1's geometry across objectives: isolated-input classification recovers 31 classes at p=0.95 and more than 50 at p=0 using target-only loss.
